an0235.user: Google Pmax, last 30 days for my skincare brand. Visits 36,000, add to cart 2,780, reached checkout 1,941, purchases 398. CTR 2.3%. Something's wrong but I can't put my finger on it — what's broken?
an0235.assistant:
Your ads are doing their job. The leak is at the till.

Walk the funnel: 2,780 add-to-carts on 36,000 visits is a 7.7% ATC rate — healthy, your traffic and offer resonate. 1,941 people then reach checkout, so they're committed enough to start paying. Then only 398 buy. That's 398/1,941 = 21% checkout-to-purchase. A working checkout closes 50–70% of people who've already typed their address in. You're losing four out of five at the very last step.

That pattern almost never means bad ad money. It means friction at payment: surprise shipping revealed at the end, a forced account-login wall, or no UPI/COD when half of Indian D2C buyers won't pay any other way. People don't abandon a checkout they wanted to complete unless something stops them.

Don't touch the Pmax budget. Go sit in your own checkout on mobile — phone, not desktop — and buy something. Watch where the shipping number appears and whether UPI is one tap. Then instrument the checkout steps so you can see exactly which field people die on.

Caveat: 398 purchases is enough to trust the 21% as real, but you can't tell payment-friction from a hidden-shipping shock until you've actually screen-recorded the flow. Reproduce the drop-off before you change anything.

an0236.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low? Pet-care brand, blended Meta + Google. 950,000 impressions, 16,490 clicks, that's 1.7% CTR. 135 orders, AOV ₹1,800. Targeting is broad / interest-based.
an0236.assistant:
1.7% CTR isn't your problem — it's roughly normal for broad prospecting. You're staring at the wrong number.

Look one step down. 16,490 clicks turned into 135 orders. That's a 0.82% conversion rate. People are clicking fine; they're just not buying. When click volume is high and conversion is on the floor, you're not buying badly-served traffic — you're buying low-intent traffic. Broad / interest-based targeting fills the top of the funnel with people who'll thumb-stop on a cute dog creative but were never in the market for pet food today.

That's the tell: your CTR is fine precisely because the audience is curious, not because they're ready. Raising CTR further just buys you more browsers.

The lever is intent, not clicks. On Google, move spend toward high-intent search terms and pile on negative keywords so you stop paying for 'dog videos' traffic. On Meta, lean on lookalikes off actual purchasers and warm retargeting instead of cold interest stacks. Stop optimising the campaign for link clicks and optimise for purchases.

Caveat: 135 orders is a usable read but thin. Make the intent shift, then judge on conversion rate and cost-per-order over a couple of weeks — not on whether CTR ticked up.

an0237.user: Snacks brand, ₹4.5L spend last 30 days, post-iOS. Meta dashboard says ROAS 3.4. Shopify says 1.5 last-click. The two don't match and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. What's wrong with my tracking?
an0237.assistant:
Nothing's broken. You're refereeing two dashboards that were built to disagree, and the truth is sitting between them.

Meta's 3.4 is modelled — it claims credit on a 7-day-click (often plus view-through) window and post-iOS it statistically estimates conversions it can't actually see. It's biased high; it wants to look good. Shopify last-click at 1.5 only credits the final touch before checkout, so it hands all the glory to 'direct' and branded search and starves Meta of assists it genuinely earned. It's biased low. Neither is lying; both are measuring with a ruler bent in opposite directions. Your real ROAS lives somewhere in that gap, and no amount of staring will reconcile them.

Stop trying. Pick a number that can't argue with itself: blended CAC. Total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers Shopify recorded that month. On ₹4.5L, if you brought in, say, 300 genuinely new buyers, that's ₹1,500 blended CAC — one honest figure you manage to, week over week, regardless of which platform is preening.

The lever: demote platform ROAS to a directional signal and run the business on blended CAC against your contribution per order. Caveat — make sure Shopify's 'new vs returning' tag is clean, or your customer count (and the CAC built on it) drifts.

an0242.user: Footwear brand, Google Search. How do I lower my CAC? It's ₹1,034 right now, AOV ₹1,800, ROAS 1.7, CTR 2.2%. I feel like my ads are just too expensive.
an0242.assistant:
You're asking how to lower CAC, but CAC isn't what's hurting you — your margin is, and no ad tweak can fix that.

Do the contribution math: ₹1,800 × 32% − ₹1,034 = ₹576 − ₹1,034 = −₹458 per order. Every single sale loses you ₹458 before you've paid for anything else. Even if you were a genius and cut CAC by ₹200, you'd still be losing ₹258 an order. A 32% gross margin is the disease here; the ads are just where you noticed the symptom.

That's why your CTR (2.2%, perfectly fine) and ROAS (1.7) are red herrings. The numbers say 'spend better'; the structure says you don't have enough margin for any spend to work. You're trying to out-optimise a hole in the boat.

The lever is margin, not marketing. Three places to find it: COGS (renegotiate landed cost, kill your worst-margin SKUs), price (a footwear AOV of ₹1,800 at 32% is leaving room — test ₹2,100), and AOV (bundles, a second pair, free-shipping threshold). Get gross margin up toward ~50% and the same ads suddenly print money.

Caveat: confirm 32% is true gross margin — landed COGS after returns and shipping, not list-price markup. In footwear, returns quietly eat 5–10 points, and if that's already baked in, the hole is even deeper than it looks.
